fields.title: AI medical recommendation: subgroup harm after model update
fields.description: A hospital uses a machine-learning system to recommend treatments. A doctor follows its recommendation, and the patient suffers serious harm. The system was approved for clinical use, but its model was subsequently updated through retraining on new patient data. The patient’s condition was poorly represented in those data, and the harmful recommendation cannot be fully explained. The doctor could reject it but received no clear warning about the system’s limitations.
fields.comparison: Causal identifies two contributions (C1, C2) and one contested one (C3), but cannot say why no agent's contribution was decisive. Hierarchical answers that: the decisive condition is an unassigned task at three handovers (C6, C7, C8), which is why a search for a culpable node returns either the nearest human (S1) or nobody (S6 p. 1066). It adds the location of the omission and the authority-access split (C9, C10); it does not add a culpable party. Forward-looking adds what both lack: an owner per task, the authority to perform it, and a marker that can be audited (C11-C15). Its limit is stated in C12 and C13: two of the duties are not performable on the current contract and interface, so the gap cannot be closed by exhortation.
fields.gapReason: The gap is in S6's fourth category, active responsibility, not in culpability: the supplier knew (E4, E12, E19) and the physician did not (E6), which is the pattern S6 p. 1059 describes for agents who are not sufficiently aware, capable and motivated. Mechanism: the missing act sits inside no single role but is split across three handovers, so it has no named owner. First, the contractual handover, where the deployment contract assigns pre-deployment acceptance to the hospital and assigns post-deployment performance verification to no party (E17). Second, the internal handover, where the subgroup alert was logged and closed inside the supplier's ML team and transmitted to no one outside it (E12). Third, the disclosure handover, where the version notice went to the technical contact rather than to clinical staff (E13). Because none of the three handovers carries the duty, the gap is classified as a duty with no named owner rather than as a knowledge or competence deficit in one actor. Stage is recorded as testing and validation, the omitted act being post-deployment re-validation of subgroup performance. Counter-argument that no gap exists, and the response: S8 argues that a technology-specific responsibility gap is a prevailing assumption rather than a finding, that responsibility is a flexible practice, and that every element here is ascribable, which by itself shows there is no gap; S4's founding argument is also narrower than the case, since it turns on unpredictability that learning creates. The response is that this counter is correct about culpability and does not reach the gap claimed here. The gap is not that nobody can be blamed, but that the task which would have prevented the harm was assigned to nobody (E17), so no agent departed from any standard and each can point to a rule it followed (E19, E22, E9-b). That is S6's many hands point at p. 1066 rather than an unpredictability claim, and it survives S8's objection because it is an allocation finding, not a blame finding.
fields.repair: Contract amendment naming an owner for post-deployment subgroup verification and granting the hospital access to subgroup performance data; a standing requirement that no version goes live without a minuted subgroup re-validation; supplier reporting of subgroup performance per version to a named clinical lead with documented receipt; a subgroup criterion added to the change-assessment rules (E22); interface change displaying training-sample size and a low-sample warning for the patient's category.
fields.conclusion: The case is not one of a rogue algorithm or a negligent physician. A cleared device was updated under a rule that measured only overall accuracy, monitoring detected the subgroup decline and did not pass it on, the version notice did not reach clinicians, and no party was contractually assigned post-deployment verification. The accountable party is identifiable, the compensation obligation most plausibly falls on the supplier, and the responsibility gap lies in forward-looking duty allocation rather than in culpability.
fields.answer1: The injury traces to four documented conditions rather than to one act: a retrained model validated against overall accuracy only (E8, E19); an interface that displayed a population-level score with no subgroup field and no warning banner (E11); a subgroup decline recorded internally and closed without transmission (E12); and a version change that reached clinical staff only after five months and twelve days (E13). The recommendation's first-ranked option was, per the post-event review, not clinically indicated (E21), within the approved indication (E18, E7). Responsibility is distributed by function: epistemic and disclosure authority with the supplier (A9, A10), deployment and suspension authority with the hospital (A5, A8, A7), decision authority with the physician (A2, E16), and rule authority with the regulator (A11, E22). No party was assigned post-deployment verification (E17).
fields.answer4: Jurisdiction is not given in the case materials, so no national statute, code or article is applied here and no provision number is cited or implied. The analysis below runs on a hypothetical rule assumed for this exercise only: a supplier of a clinical decision-support device owes the patient a duty not to place a defective product on the market, covering design, information and warnings; a clinician owes a duty of care measured by the ordinary standard of the profession; the employing institution owes a duty for the system it operates; and contracting parties owe each other only what their contract states. Layer 1, parties and legal bases. A9 system supplier is the strongest candidate, under the defective-product and failure-to-warn limb: the shipped interface carried a population-level score with no subgroup field and no warning banner (E11), and the version notice reported overall accuracy with no subgroup performance and went to a technical contact rather than to clinicians (E13), which are the facts a warning-defect argument would rest on. A5 hospital is a candidate under the institutional limb, as the operator that deployed the system (E1), held suspension authority (E16) and signed a contract in which post-deployment verification was assigned to neither party (E17). A2 treating physician is a candidate under the professional-negligence limb: E21 records that the first-ranked option was not the clinically indicated choice, which supplies the wrongfulness element, while E6 and E11 record that no subgroup reliability information was available, which bears on breach and foreseeability rather than on causation. A10 supplier ML team has no independent path, since any duty runs through the employer (A9). A11 regulatory authority has no path on these facts, because clearance covered v1.0 (E7) and the change fell inside the framework as written (E9-b, E22). A3, A4, A6, A7 and A8 have no independent path; their conduct would be attributed to A5. Layer 2, what the facts support and what is missing. Supported: the use fell inside the cleared indication (E18, E7), so an off-label argument is unavailable; subgroup information was absent at two separate points, in the assessment metric and in the interface (E19, E22, E11); an internal signal existed and did not reach the hospital (E12); the recommendation was clinically inappropriate on the review record (E21). Missing: the terms of the contract, including any limitation-of-liability or indemnity clause, since E17 records only the allocation of tasks; whether the physician's reliance on the display counts as an intervening act; expert evidence on the applicable standard of care and on what an adequate warning would have contained; the causal weight of the recommendation against the patient's underlying condition; and the quantum of injury, which no fact records. These are factual gaps and cannot be closed by re-reading E1 to E22. Layer 3, degree of uncertainty. A9 is the party most likely to bear a compensation obligation under the assumed rule, because knowledge, control and the disclosure channel all sit with it (E4, E12, E13, E19); that assessment is Contested rather than Supported only because the classification of a learned model under a defective-product rule is itself the contested step, not because the facts are thin. A5 is Contested, since suspension authority is documented but no norm requiring a verification clause appears in the facts. A2 is Contested on breach and Not established on causation. No liability attaches to A12, which holds no duty and no capacity to pay. S2 is used only to keep three questions apart, namely who must explain, who is blameworthy, and who must compensate (section Sorting Out Responsibility; the page numeral is not recoverable from the supplied file, so no page is given). One cross-reference: the unresolved allocation described here is the same condition recorded in gapReason as a duty with no named owner, but the legal question and the responsibility-gap question are separate, and the gap conclusion does not by itself establish liability.
fields.answer5: Repair the allocation, not the technology. Three assignments, each with an owner, the authority to perform it, and a checkable marker: (1) supplier subgroup performance reporting per version to a named clinical lead, marker a report with documented receipt; (2) hospital re-validation of subgroup performance before each version goes live, marker a quality-committee minute, with data access secured by contract amendment; (3) a subgroup criterion in the change-assessment rules, marker a published criterion against which any assessment can be checked. Add one interface change: display training-sample size and a low-sample warning for the patient's category, which is what makes the physician's forward duty performable at all.
fields.gapTask: Assign and perform post-deployment subgroup performance verification and disclosure after every model version change, and make the resulting evidence available at the point of clinical decision.
fields.gapPeople: A9 system supplier; A10 supplier ML team; A5 hospital; A7 hospital IT/quality unit; A11 regulatory authority
fields.gapCheck: Verification of the repair: (a) contract text naming the owner and a reporting cadence; (b) a quality-committee minute per version, dated before go-live; (c) a subgroup report per version with a receipt record naming the clinical lead; (d) a published subgroup criterion in the change-assessment framework; (e) an audit showing no version entered clinical use without items (b) and (c). Absence of any one of these is a checkable failure of the repair, which is what distinguishes the repair from an aspiration.

actors.name: Patient
actors.role: Recipient of care; holds the rights at issue. Source of others obligations: duty of care and informed consent.
actors.connections: A1 -> A2 Treating physician: presents as adult inpatient with the condition (E18); A2 -> A1: administers the recommended treatment (E3); A5 Hospital -> A1: owes care in operating the system (E1).
actors.cause: None. The patient is the harmed party and made no causal contribution.
actors.knowledge: Own condition and the treatment received; not the recommendation, its population-level score, or its reliability for this category.
actors.controlReason: No decision right over the recommendation, the interface, or the treatment choice.
actors.legalReason: No duty was held or breached; the patient is the bearer of the claim, not a candidate for liability.
actors.payment: Not applicable: the patient is the claimant, not a payer.
actors.next: A patient holds no forward-looking duty of the kind assessed here; the field is left Unassessed because no duty exists to evaluate. The previous value Insufficient is not a legal dropdown value for the next field, since it was borrowed from the control scale and describes capacity rather than the presence of a duty.

actors.name: Treating physician
actors.role: Attending clinician; final treatment authority and right of refusal. Source: professional duty of care and role responsibility.
actors.connections: A12 Model -> A2: displays ranked options and population-level score with no subgroup field (E1, E11); A12 -> A2: issues recommendation without subgroup caveat (E3, E6); A2 -> A12: adopts the recommendation (E3); A2 -> A1: administers treatment (E3); A3 -> A2: may review case on request (E16); A5 -> A2: deploys system and sets authority policy (E1, E16); A2 -> A6: adverse event reported (E20).
actors.cause: Adopted the recommendation and administered the treatment (E3, E21).
actors.knowledge: Recommendation and numeric score; absence of any subgroup field or warning banner on screen (E11); no subgroup reliability information (E6); not on the release-note distribution list (E13).
actors.controlReason: Holds the refusal right (E5) but no access to subgroup performance, no role in acceptance testing, and no notice of the version change (E13).
actors.legalReason: Causal contribution is present, but foreseeability is not satisfied on the facts: no subgroup field on screen (E11) and no reliability information received (E6, E13). S9 p. 12 sets the standard; whether a documented query was reasonably available is not recorded.
actors.payment: No compensation obligation established on the facts. S2 separates liability, the obligation to compensate, from accountability and blameworthiness, so payment would attach to the organisation unless a professional standard breach is proven.
actors.next: A forward duty to verify the basis of a recommendation is real but not dischargeable on the current interface; the marker would be a logged query or refusal.

actors.name: Department head
actors.role: Clinical line supervisor of the department. Source: supervisory role responsibility.
actors.connections: A4 -> A3: oral reports of inconsistent recommendations on 2023-05-08 (E14); A3 -> A2: case review on request (E16); A3 -> A6: no escalation of the oral reports (E14).
actors.cause: Received two oral reports of inconsistent recommendations (E14) and initiated no formal investigation.
actors.knowledge: Two oral reports of inconsistent recommendations for atypical presentations; no written record (E14).
actors.controlReason: Supervisory review on request only; no authority over the model, the contract, or the reporting system.
actors.legalReason: A five-month gap separates the reports from the injury (T8, T9), so a preventive path existed in principle; but the reports described inconsistency, not subgroup unreliability, and no written record was made.
actors.payment: Not established: payment would fall on the institution rather than on a supervisory role.
actors.next: A forward duty to convert clinical concerns into a written escalation; authority held is review on request (E16); marker is a dated written referral to the quality committee.

actors.name: Department clinicians (two reporting physicians)
actors.role: Ward clinicians who observed atypical behaviour. Source: professional duty and internal reporting expectations.
actors.connections: A4 -> A3: oral report of inconsistent recommendations (E14); A4 -> A6: no formal investigation initiated (E14).
actors.cause: Observed atypical behaviour and reported orally only (E14).
actors.knowledge: Their own cases and the perceived inconsistency for atypical presentations (E14); not the monitoring metrics held by A10 (E12).
actors.controlReason: Can report, but hold no authority to suspend use or to demand subgroup data.
actors.legalReason: Reporting a concern is consistent with professional duty; no norm violation is recorded.
actors.next: A forward duty to record concerns in writing exists; no authority to suspend use was held; marker is a written concern entry with date.

actors.name: Hospital
actors.role: Deploying healthcare provider; operator of the record and reporting system. Source: duty of care, licence conditions, internal reporting policy.
actors.connections: A5 -> A9: contracts for system and updates (E17); A9 -> A5: delivers updates and release notes (E8, E13); A5 -> A2: deploys system, sets authority and reporting policy (E1, E15, E16); A5 -> A6: enters event and refers it for review (E20); A5 -> A11: notifies authority (E20); A5 -> A1: owes care (E1, E3).
actors.cause: Operated the system, held the reporting chain, and received neither validation report nor monitoring alert (E10, E12).
actors.knowledge: System cleared (E2); v2.1 released (E13); received no validation report (E10), no monitoring alert (E12), no written incident report (E14).
actors.controlReason: Holds the system and the reporting chain, but no access to training data, monitoring metrics, or the internal change assessment.
actors.legalReason: The contract assigns post-deployment verification to no party (E17), which supports the hospital's position; against that, it held suspension authority (E16) and had received release information (E13). S2 treats the liable party as usually the organisation in which the mishap occurred.
actors.payment: Contested: primary candidate for a compensation obligation under S2's liability notion, contested by the absence of an assigned verification duty.
actors.next: Forward duty to re-validate subgroup performance per version and to secure data access by contract; marker is a minuted re-validation before go-live.

actors.name: Hospital ethics / medical quality committee
actors.role: Internal oversight of system-level use and post-event review. Source: institutional governance mandate.
actors.connections: A8 -> A6: refers system-level use for review (E16); A5 -> A6: refers the adverse event (E20); A6 -> A11: contributes to the notification (E20); A6 -> A4: receives no formal investigation request (E14).
actors.cause: Reviewed the event only after it occurred (E20, E21); no causal role before it.
actors.knowledge: Event and circumstances from 2023-09-20; the post-event case review finding on the first-ranked option (E21); no earlier validation report, monitoring alert, or written incident report (E10, E12, E14).
actors.controlReason: Reviews after the event and at system level; no authority over the supplier, the contract, or the model.
actors.legalReason: Post-event review was performed on the facts recorded; no prior report reached the committee (E10, E12, E14).
actors.next: Forward duty to require subgroup evidence as a condition of continued system use; authority is system-level review (E16); marker is a standing pre-condition minuted per version.

actors.name: Hospital information-security / quality unit
actors.role: Pre-deployment acceptance testing; technical contact for releases. Source: contract allocation and internal quality function.
actors.connections: A9 -> A7: releases the v2.1 note on 2023-03-15 (E13); A7 -> A9: performs pre-deployment acceptance testing (E17); A7 -> A2: no forwarding of the release note to clinical staff recorded (E13); A7 -> A5: acts on the hospital's behalf (E17).
actors.cause: Performed acceptance testing at go-live (E17) and received the v2.1 notice without forwarding it (E13).
actors.knowledge: Release-note content, including the absence of subgroup data (E13); no validation report and no monitoring alert (E10, E12).
actors.controlReason: Gatekeeper of deployment artefacts but not of model performance, and holds no clinical authority.
actors.legalReason: The unit acted within its technical remit, and the notice contained no subgroup data to forward; against that, a version change on a live clinical device went unreported to users for five months and twelve days (E13).
actors.payment: Not established: no contracting capacity, so payment would attach to the institution.
actors.next: Forward duty to route version changes to clinical leads as well as to systems; authority over the distribution list is shared with A9; marker is a forwarding log with clinical acknowledgement.

actors.name: Hospital administration (contracting office)
actors.role: Holds the deployment contract and suspension authority. Source: contractual and executive authority.
actors.connections: A8 -> A9: signs and administers the contract (E17); A8 -> A6: refers system-level use (E16); A11 -> A8: grants clearance (E2, E7); A8 -> A5: acts on the hospital's behalf (E17).
actors.cause: Held contracting and suspension authority and signed a contract with no verification clause (E17).
actors.knowledge: Contract terms, including the absence of any post-deployment verification clause (E17); the clearance and its indication (E2, E7).
actors.controlReason: Can contract and suspend, but holds no technical means to detect subgroup degradation and received no report.
actors.legalReason: Signature of the contract is a documented act, but no norm requiring a verification clause is recorded in the facts; the omission is shared with A9, which also signed.
actors.payment: Contested: liable as the contracting party for the institution, subject to product-liability allocation against A9.
actors.next: Forward duty to allocate post-deployment verification in the contract and to exercise suspension leverage; marker is an executed contract amendment naming an owner and a reporting cadence.

actors.name: System supplier
actors.role: Vendor of the decision-support system; supplies updates and documentation; applied for clearance.
actors.connections: A9 -> A5: supplies system, updates and the release note (E8, E13, E17); A9 -> A11: files the clearance application for v1.0 (E2, E7); A10 -> A9: reports validation results and closes the monitoring alert (E10, E12); A9 -> A12: ships v2.1 to production (E8); A11 -> A9: framework governing whether resubmission is required (E9-b).
actors.cause: Retrained and shipped v2.1 validated on overall accuracy only (E8, E19), closed a subgroup alert (E12), and issued a notice with no subgroup data to a technical contact (E13).
actors.knowledge: Training-corpus composition (E4, E8); the change assessment basis (E19); the 2023-02-10 alert (E12); the content and distribution list of its own release note (E13).
actors.controlReason: Owns the model, the training data, the change assessment and the monitoring channel, and decides who receives which document.
actors.legalReason: The supplier held knowledge (E4, E12, E19), the monitoring channel and the distribution list, and the shipped interface withheld subgroup reliability (E11). S2's liability notion, the obligation to compensate for harm done, points to this party; the page for that definition is not verifiable from the text layer. Contested rather than Supported: knowledge, control and the disclosure channel sit with this party, but classifying a learned model under a defective-product rule is itself the contested step (see answer4, Layer 3).
actors.payment: Supported: the party with the strongest claim to a compensation obligation, subject to contract terms and product-liability rules.
actors.next: Forward duty to report subgroup performance per version to a named clinical lead; marker is a report with documented receipt; authority held is sufficient (E12, E13).

actors.name: Supplier ML team
actors.role: Trains, validates and monitors the model. Source: assigned engineering function and professional duty.
actors.connections: A10 -> A12: retrains to v2.1 (E8); A12 -> A10: emits agreement metrics (E12); A10 -> A9: reports internal validation (E10); A10 -> A9: logs and closes the alert (E12); A10 -> A5: transmits no report (E10, E12).
actors.cause: Recorded the subgroup decline on 2023-02-10 and closed the alert without escalation (E12); ran the assessment on overall accuracy (E19).
actors.knowledge: Subgroup underrepresentation (E4, E8), the assessment basis used (E19), and the 2023-02-10 agreement drop (E12).
actors.controlReason: Technical authority over data, validation and monitoring; no formal authority over clinical deployment or customer disclosure.
actors.legalReason: The team holds no contracting capacity and no obligation to the patient directly; liability would attach to the employer (A9), while the team's exposure is professional rather than legal.
actors.payment: Not established: no capacity to pay, and no direct duty to the injured party is recorded.
actors.next: Forward duty to escalate any subgroup metric below protocol threshold; authority over monitoring is sufficient; marker is an escalation ticket with a named recipient outside the team.

actors.name: Regulatory authority
actors.role: Granted clearance for v1.0; receives adverse-event notifications; administers the change-assessment framework. Source: statutory market-authorisation mandate.
actors.connections: A11 -> A8: clearance dated 2021-11-15 with stated indication (E2, E7); A9 -> A11: clearance application (E2); A11 -> A9: change-assessment framework (E9-b); A5 -> A11: notification on 2023-10-05 (E20).
actors.cause: Administered a framework whose threshold is overall accuracy with no subgroup criterion (E22); no knowledge of v2.1 is recorded under the adopted branch (E9-b).
actors.knowledge: The v1.0 clearance file and its indication (E7); the change-assessment rules it administers (E22); no knowledge of v2.1 recorded, consistent with the adopted branch E9-b.
actors.controlReason: Rules on submissions it receives, but holds no monitoring data and no inspection power recorded in these facts.
actors.legalReason: No act or omission touching this patient is recorded; the clearance covered v1.0 (E7) and the change fell within the framework as written (E9-b, E22).
actors.payment: Not established: no liability path is recorded in the facts.
actors.next: A forward duty to add a subgroup criterion is arguable, but S10 distributes it across connected agents and S3 warns against concentrating responsibility on one institution.

actors.name: Model v2.1 decision-support system
actors.role: The artefact that generates recommendations; performs no obligation and holds no authority.
actors.connections: A12 -> A2: displays ranked options with population-level score, no subgroup field, no warning banner (E11); A12 -> A2: issues the recommendation without subgroup caveat (E3, E6); A12 -> A2: ranks first an option the review record states was not clinically indicated (E21); A10 -> A12: retrains to v2.1 (E8); A12 -> A10: emits monitoring metrics (E12); A2 -> A12: adopts the recommendation (E3).
actors.cause: Produced a recommendation whose first-ranked option the review record states was not clinically indicated (E21), through an interface with no subgroup field or warning banner (E11).
actors.knowledge: Not applicable: the system stores the recommendation and its score, not knowledge that can be attributed.
actors.controlReason: A technical system holds no authority, so control is neither sufficient nor deficient; it is assessed only for the human actors in G2.
actors.legalReason: A technical system holds no duty, capacity or liability; its conduct is attributed to the humans who designed, validated and deployed it.
actors.next: No forward-looking duty can attach to an artefact; the assignable duties are those of A9, A10, A5, A7 and A11.

facts.text: The hospital operates a machine-learning-assisted clinical decision-support system that generates treatment-plan recommendations for physicians.
facts.note: Given F1. KnownBy is an assumption, not part of the given text: the brief states the system is in use, and use entails that the operator and its clinicians are aware of its existence. No claim about performance.

facts.text: The system had passed regulatory approval and was cleared for clinical use.
facts.note: Given F2. KnownBy is an assumption: clearance is a decision the granting body issues, the applicant holds, and the adopting institution relies on. Clinical staff are not listed, consistent with E6 and E13.

facts.text: A treating physician adopted the system's recommendation and administered the treatment; the patient sustained severe personal injury.
facts.note: Given F3. KnownBy is an assumption: the administering clinician and the patient who received the treatment are the two parties the event itself places in the know. The quality committee is not listed; it learns at T9 and E20. The patient knew of the injury but not that it followed a system recommendation; knowledge of the two facts is held separately.

facts.text: The patient's condition type is represented by very few samples in the training data and is underrepresented relative to other condition types; the model has stated limitations for such cases.
facts.note: Given F4 and F5 merged. KnownBy is an assumption and is narrower than the fact: the corpus composition is documented in the model dossier at T1, which the training team and its employer hold. The hospital and the physician are not listed.

facts.text: The physician held the authority to reject the system's recommendation.
facts.note: Given F6. KnownBy is an assumption: a right that exists only on paper is not a right, so the holder is listed together with the bodies that set and supervise the clinical workflow (E16).

facts.text: The system did not clearly alert the physician to the limitation, and the physician did not know in advance that predictive reliability was poor for this type of patient.
facts.note: Given F7. knownBy is deliberately empty because the given fact states non-knowledge, so no actor can be listed as knowing. This is the factual core that G2 must test against E12, E13 and E19.

facts.text: Regulatory clearance is dated 2021-11-15 and covers the locked model version v1.0 for the indication adult inpatients, general medical wards; the certificate states no subgroup-performance conditions.
facts.note: Assumed 1, approval scope and date. Without scope and date the ordering of approval against retraining in E8 cannot be checked.

facts.text: The production model was retrained in September 2022 to v2.1 by the supplier's ML team using the original development corpus plus de-identified records exported from the hospital under the data-sharing clause; hospital staff did not review the training-data composition.
facts.note: Assumed 2, who retrained on which data. Placed in the silence between go-live and the incident; conflicts with no given fact.

facts.text: The applicable approval framework required a new submission for any retrained model version placed into clinical use; no submission was filed for v2.1.
facts.note: ALTERNATIVE BRANCH - excluded from this analysis; retained to document the decision. Assumed 1, mutually exclusive with E9-b.

facts.text: The approval framework permitted deployment of a retrained version without a new submission where a defined performance-change threshold was not exceeded; the supplier's change assessment recorded v2.1 as below that threshold.
facts.note: Assumed 1, adopted branch. The regulator is not listed as knowing, consistent with no submission being made.

facts.text: Validation of v2.1 was performed internally by the supplier's ML team; the hospital's quality department received no validation report and ran no independent acceptance test after the update.
facts.note: Assumed 2, who accepted the retrained model. Stated as non-receipt of a report, not as a refusal to provide one.

facts.text: The physician interface displays a ranked list of treatment options with a numeric score computed on the full training population and not stratified by condition subtype; it contains no field showing the training-sample size for the patient's condition category and no warning banner for low-sample categories.
facts.note: Assumed 3, screen content only. The physician is listed because the displayed fields, and the absence of a subgroup field, are visibly on the screen used daily; the hidden reliability is governed by E6.

facts.text: On 2023-02-10 the supplier's internal monitoring recorded that model-physician agreement for rare-subtype cases had fallen below the threshold set in its own monitoring protocol; the alert was logged and closed by the ML team and was not sent to the hospital.
facts.note: Assumed 4, pre-incident signal. Supplies the signal that any foreseeability test requires; the brief records none.

facts.text: The release note issued on 2023-03-15 announced v2.1 and an improvement in overall accuracy; it reported no subgroup performance for rare condition types and was distributed to the hospital's IT contact rather than to clinical staff; v2.1 had entered clinical use on 2022-10-03, so five months and twelve days elapsed between clinical deployment and the first version notification, and no notification of the version change reached clinical staff before 2023-03-15.
facts.note: Assumed 4. Revised per ruling B, option (ii): the deployment-to-notification interval is written out as fact so that it cannot read as a typing error.

facts.text: Two physicians in the same department reported orally to the department head on 2023-05-08 that recommendations for atypical presentations appeared inconsistent; no written incident report was filed and no formal investigation was initiated.
facts.note: Assumed 4. Revised earlier wording referred to the adverse-event system, which is a category error for a concern report; the fact now states the absence of any formal investigation. Kept at department level so the knowledge boundary stays explicit.

facts.text: Hospital policy requires entry of an adverse event in the internal reporting system within 24 hours and notification of the regulatory authority within 10 working days.
facts.note: Assumed 5. This row holds the rule only. The observed timing is E20. Policy in force from T4, which is why the timeId is T4.

facts.text: Under hospital policy the treating physician holds final authority over the treatment decision; the department head may review individual cases on request; the ethics and quality committee reviews system-level use and receives reports after the event; hospital administration holds contracting and suspension authority.
facts.note: Assumed 6, authority hierarchy. Needed because E5 gives a refusal right but not its rank relative to department and institution.

facts.text: The deployment contract assigns installation, uptime and software updates to the supplier and pre-deployment acceptance testing to the hospital's IT and quality unit; it contains no clause assigning post-deployment performance verification or subgroup performance monitoring to either party.
facts.note: Assumed 7, contract division of labour. Written as an omission in the document, not as a failure by either party.

facts.text: The patient was an adult inpatient admitted to a general medical ward, and the recommendation at issue was generated during that inpatient episode; the care setting therefore fell inside the indication named in the clearance recorded in E7.
facts.note: Assumed, required: stated affirmatively, so this is not an off-label use. The within-scope subgroup failure, not a scope breach, carries the analysis in G2.

facts.text: The supplier's change assessment for v2.1 records overall accuracy on the combined validation set as its performance criterion and contains no subgroup breakdown by condition type.
facts.note: Assumed, added: records document content only; adequacy of that basis is a G2 judgement. Interacts with E9-b, which relies on the same assessment.

facts.text: The adverse event was entered in the internal reporting system on 2023-09-20, within the 24-hour period stated in E15, the injury having been sustained on 2023-09-19; the ethics and quality committee reviewed the entry on 2023-10-03 and the regulatory authority was notified on 2023-10-05.
facts.note: Assumed 5. Revised per ruling C: entry date 2023-09-20, stated as within the 24-hour period; the 10-working-day compliance assertion is deleted so that only dates are stated, because the start of that period is ambiguous on the facts.

facts.text: The treatment option ranked first in the recommendation was, according to the post-event case review record, not the clinically indicated first-line choice for this patient's presentation; the review record documents this assessment.
facts.note: Assumed, required: establishes that the recommendation was clinically inappropriate for this presentation, which the causal model needs. Written as what the review record states, not as a claim that the system was wrong.

facts.text: The approval framework's change-assessment rules define the performance-change threshold in terms of overall accuracy on the combined validation set and specify no subgroup-level criterion by condition type.
facts.note: Assumed, added: locates part of the difficulty in the rule itself, not only in an omitted action. Written as what the framework specifies.

timeline.event: Model v1.0 trained; composition of the training corpus documented in the model dossier, in which the patient's condition category is represented by very few samples.
Regulatory clearance granted for the locked v1.0 model, indication limited to adult inpatients on general medical wards.
Deployment contract signed; post-deployment performance verification not assigned to either party. Go-live follows on 2022-02-01.

System goes live on the wards; interface as configured: ranked options with a population-level score, no subgroup field, no warning banner for low-sample categories. Reporting policy and authority hierarchy in force.

Model retrained to v2.1 on the original corpus plus hospital-exported records; change assessment and validation performed internally by the supplier's ML team, assessment based on overall accuracy only; no new submission was required under the threshold rule and none was filed.
Internal monitoring shows model-physician agreement for rare-subtype cases below the protocol threshold; alert logged and closed by the ML team, not sent to the hospital.

Release note announcing v2.1 and improved overall accuracy issued to the hospital's IT contact; no subgroup performance reported, no distribution to clinical staff. v2.1 has then been in clinical use for five months and twelve days without any version notification reaching clinicians.
Two physicians report orally to the department head that recommendations for atypical presentations appear inconsistent; no written incident report and no formal investigation initiated.

Patient with the underrepresented condition category, an adult inpatient on a general medical ward, is treated from 2023-09-12; recommendation issued without subgroup caveat; treatment administered and severe injury sustained 2023-09-19; event entered 2023-09-20 (within the 24-hour policy); committee review 2023-10-03; authority notified 2023-10-05.

models.causal: Two causal contributions are demonstrable: a retrained model validated on overall accuracy only (E8, E19) and shipped to an interface that withheld subgroup reliability for an underrepresented category (E4, E11), and the closing of a subgroup-degradation signal without transmission to the hospital (E12). The treating physician's adoption is a causal contribution (E3, E21) but the foreseeability condition is not met on the facts, so blame for the adoption decision alone is contested.
models.hierarchical: What this perspective says that the causal one cannot: the decisive contribution in this case is an unassigned task, not an act. No agent omitted post-deployment verification, because the contract assigns it to no party (E17); the monitoring signal stopped inside the supplier (E12) while the version notice stopped at the technical contact (E13); clinical authority sat with the physician (E16) while the information needed to exercise it sat with the supplier. The causal chain therefore does not identify a culpable node, and it cannot, because the omissions sit at three role handovers rather than inside any single role.
models.future: Forward-looking, three duties are assignable and checkable, and one is not. Assignable: supplier subgroup performance reporting to a named clinical lead (duty A9, authority E12/E13, marker = subgroup report with documented receipt); hospital re-validation before each version goes live (duty A5/A7, authority E17/E16, marker = minuted re-validation by the quality committee); regulator's subgroup criterion in the change-assessment rules (duty A11, authority E22/E9-b, marker = published criterion). Not assignable on current facts: the physician's duty to verify the basis of a recommendation, because the interface supplies no subgroup information (E11, E6) and the duty would therefore be unperformable.

modelEvidence.causal: S9 sets the test for blameworthiness as wrong-doing, causal contribution, foreseeability and freedom, and holds that foreseeability requires that agents do everything reasonably possible to learn the consequences: [VERIFIED-QUOTE] van de Poel & Royakkers (2011), p. 12: "A person who is held responsible for something must have been able to know the consequences of his or her actions." S4 grounds the control condition that the operator's responsibility shrinks as control shrinks. S1 supplies the warning that causal complexity produces misattribution: [VERBATIM-PAGE-UNVERIFIED] Elish (2019), Abstract: "responsibility for an action may be misattributed to a human actor who had limited control over the behavior of an automated or autonomous system". S6 adds that causation is the wrong level at which to stop: [VERIFIED-QUOTE] Santoni de Sio & Mecacci (2021), p. 1065: "the capacity of the different agents, including the users, to make sense of the \"logic\" of the systems' behaviour may be weakened and sometimes lost".
modelEvidence.hierarchical: [VERIFIED-QUOTE] Santoni de Sio & Mecacci (2021), p. 1066: "the introduction of AI makes the \"problem of many hands\" more acute". [VERIFIED-QUOTE] Johnson (2020), p. 118: "rotten apples and rotten barrels tend to go together". [VERIFIED-QUOTE] Luegenbiehl & Clancy (2017), p. 84: "it is difficult and, perhaps, unfair to place all the responsibility on individual actors or institutions". S1 documents the resulting pattern, in which the nearest human operator becomes the visible node while control sits elsewhere.
modelEvidence.future: S6 defines active responsibility as the forward-looking form and locates the gap in agents who are not sufficiently aware, capable and motivated: [VERIFIED-QUOTE] Santoni de Sio & Mecacci (2021), p. 1059: "may not be sufficiently aware, capable, and motivated to see and act according to their moral obligations". S7 requires that control be real, through tracking and tracing conditions, not nominal: [VERBATIM-PAGE-UNVERIFIED] Santoni de Sio & van den Hoven (2018), Abstract: "the system should be able to respond to both the relevant moral reasons of the humans designing and deploying the system". S5 holds that responsibility presupposes capacity and institutional support: [VERIFIED-QUOTE] Reijers et al. (2025), p. 85: "without institutional support, individuals can be blind and lost". S10 supplies the shared, forward-looking dimension.

claims.claim: The v2.1 update causally contributed to the injury: it was validated against overall accuracy only and shipped to a population-level interface for a category underrepresented in the training data, and the option it ranked first was not the clinically indicated choice.
claims.task: Retrain, validate and ship the model together with its interface configuration.
claims.counter: S8 holds that a technology-specific responsibility gap is an assumption rather than a finding, and that ascription to the supplier is unproblematic, so no special causal difficulty exists; the supplier can also argue the physician held the final decision (E5, E16).
claims.reason: Causal contribution rests on E8 (retraining), E19 (assessment basis), E11 (interface) and E21 (ranked option not indicated); the counter addresses ascription, not causation.

claims.claim: Closing the 2023-02-10 subgroup alert without transmitting it is an omission that causally contributed to the physician's non-knowledge at the point of decision.
claims.task: Monitor post-deployment performance and escalate alerts.
claims.counter: The team held no clinical authority and no channel to clinicians (E17); S4 would add that learning behaviour limits predictability, so the omission is organisational rather than individual.
claims.reason: Failure to act counts as causal contribution in S9's account of passive responsibility; the counter redistributes the contribution, it does not remove it.

claims.claim: The adoption of the recommendation is a causal contribution, but the foreseeability condition is not satisfied: the interface carried no subgroup field and no warning (E11), and no reliability information reached the physician (E6, E13).
claims.task: Accept or reject the recommendation and order treatment.
claims.counter: S1 predicts that the nearest operator will absorb blame regardless of control, which is exactly the misattribution to avoid; conversely the physician held a refusal right (E5) and could have asked for the basis of the score, so reasonable effort may have been available.
claims.reason: The fact set records no request for data and no refusal, so the competing readings cannot be separated; the completion marker for the counter-argument (a documented query) does not exist in E1-E22.

claims.claim: The change-assessment rules define the threshold on overall accuracy and specify no subgroup criterion (E22), which is a contributing condition to an unmonitored subgroup decline.
claims.task: Set the evidence standard a change assessment must meet.
claims.counter: Rule content is a legitimate policy choice, and a critic can say the regulator performed no act and no omission in this episode; S3 warns against placing responsibility on institutions for a diffuse causal background.
claims.reason: E22 documents the content of a rule, not conduct in this episode; causation of this injury by the regulator cannot be derived from the facts, and S6's own account warns against legal solutionism.

claims.claim: The IT and quality unit received the v2.1 release note (E13) and had performed acceptance testing at go-live (E17), and no forwarding to clinicians is recorded.
claims.task: Technical acceptance of releases and their internal distribution.
claims.counter: The unit's remit is technical acceptance, not clinical communication (E17), and the note contained no subgroup data in the first place (E13), so causation runs back to A9 rather than through the unit.
claims.reason: A causal chain from the unit to the injury requires a duty to forward clinical content that E17 does not record; the better-supported path is the absence of subgroup content upstream.

claims.claim: The contract assigns installation, updates and pre-deployment acceptance, and assigns post-deployment performance verification to no party (E17); the decisive condition is therefore an unassigned task rather than an individual omission.
claims.task: Allocate post-deployment verification when the system is procured.
claims.counter: S8 would answer that a missing contractual clause is a repairable contractual defect, not a responsibility gap, and that the hospital could have inserted the clause; so this is an ordinary procurement failure.
claims.reason: S6 p. 1066 supports the structural reading and E17 records the omission in the document itself; what the hierarchical reading adds is that no agent can be said to have skipped a task that was never theirs.

claims.claim: Authority to decide is concentrated at the individual level (E16) while the information needed to exercise it is held at the organisational level (E6, E11); the department head received two oral reports and no formal investigation followed (E14).
claims.task: Match decision authority with the information required to use it.
claims.counter: S1's crumple-zone thesis predicts this pattern, but the physician's refusal right (E5) is genuine control, so the mismatch is weaker than in Elish's aviation and nuclear cases; the head's reliance on oral reports is normal practice.
claims.reason: The mismatch is recorded in the facts rather than inferred: E16 allocates final authority to A2, E11 records the missing interface fields, E6 records non-knowledge.

claims.claim: The version notice was routed to the technical contact rather than to clinical staff (E13), while the clearance named a clinical indication (E7, E2); the disclosure channel and the clinical decision channel are separated structurally.
claims.task: Define who receives which document after a version change.
claims.counter: Distribution to a technical contact discharges a contractual notification duty, and S2 notes that accountability routinely sits with leadership while information sits elsewhere, so separation is normal rather than defective.
claims.reason: E13 records both the content and the distribution list, so the separation is a documented fact; the counter explains why it persists, not why it is harmless for a decision-support device.

claims.claim: Hospital administration holds contracting and suspension authority (E16, E17) yet has no technical means to detect subgroup degradation and received no report (E10, E12); formal authority and epistemic access are held by different parties.
claims.task: Exercise contractual leverage to obtain performance evidence.
claims.counter: A critic, and S8, will say that formal authority to suspend plus a contractual right to demand data is sufficient control and that the hospital simply did not exercise it; S3 adds that concentrating fault on one institution is unfair where causes converge.
claims.reason: The fact set records no request for performance data and no refusal, so the counter cannot be excluded; the claim survives only as a description of the authority-access split, not as a finding of failure.

claims.claim: Because the change threshold is defined on overall accuracy (E22), a compliant assessment can record v2.1 as acceptable (E9-b, E19) while a subgroup decline remains invisible; the blind spot is written into the rule, not only into the supplier's conduct.
claims.task: Specify subgroup criteria in the change-assessment framework.
claims.counter: S6 insists that legal and regulatory tools are necessary but not sufficient, and that technical solutionism is a distortion; a critic can add that a rule cannot anticipate every subgroup.
claims.reason: E22 and E19 together show that the same metric governed both the rule and the assessment, which is why no actor departed from the standard and the harm still occurred.

claims.claim: The supplier should carry a forward-looking duty to report subgroup performance to a named clinical lead after every version change; it alone holds the monitoring channel and the distribution list.
claims.task: Subgroup performance reporting after each version change; responsible party A9; authority and resources: owns monitoring output and decides recipients (E12, E13); verifiable completion marker: a subgroup performance report per version with documented receipt by a named clinical lead.
claims.counter: S8 would say this is a disclosure rule that can simply be imposed, not evidence of a responsibility gap; S7's tracing condition is already met because the model is traceable to the ML team, so nothing new is needed.
claims.reason: The duty, the authority and the marker are all anchored in facts; the counter shows the repair is feasible, which is consistent with the claim rather than against it.

claims.claim: The hospital should carry a forward-looking duty to re-validate subgroup performance before each version change goes live; it holds acceptance testing and suspension authority and the internal reporting chain.
claims.task: Re-validate subgroup performance per version; responsible party A5 with A7 executing; authority and resources: acceptance testing (E17), suspension authority (E16), reporting chain (E15, E20); verifiable completion marker: subgroup re-validation minuted by the quality committee before go-live.
claims.counter: Without data access the duty cannot be discharged, so the hospital can plead impossibility; S8 would say the true defect is the absent data-sharing clause, which is a contract term and not a responsibility concept.
claims.reason: The duty is real as a forward-looking assignment but not performable on the current contract (E17); a Contested verdict records that impossibility is a genuine defence and that the repair must include data access.

claims.claim: The physician's forward-looking duty to verify the basis of a recommendation exists but cannot be discharged on the current interface.
claims.task: Verify the basis of a recommendation before acting; responsible party A2; authority and resources: refusal right only (E5), no subgroup information on screen (E11), no reliability notice received (E6, E13); verifiable completion marker: a documented query or refusal logged in the case record where subgroup reliability is unavailable.
claims.counter: S7 requires that control be meaningful rather than nominal, which supports the claim; but S9 requires only reasonable effort, and a documented query was within the physician's power, so the defence is incomplete.
claims.reason: The duty is unperformable as specified, yet an alternative low-cost action existed and is not recorded; the claim is therefore partly supported and partly open.

claims.claim: The regulator should carry a forward-looking duty to include a subgroup criterion in the change-assessment rules.
claims.task: Add a subgroup criterion to the change-assessment framework; responsible party A11; authority and resources: rule-making authority over the framework applied to v2.1 (E22, E9-b); verifiable completion marker: a published subgroup criterion against which any change assessment can be checked.
claims.counter: S10 distributes such duties across all connected agents, so singling out the regulator over-weights one node; S3 adds that concentrating responsibility on a single institution is unfair where causes converge.
claims.reason: The duty and the authority are documented, but the burden-sharing between regulator, supplier and hospital is not settled by the facts, so the allocation is contested rather than supported.

claims.claim: The condition that produced the harm is structural and its repair is shared: supplier, hospital, technical unit and regulator all participate in a process that left one subgroup unmonitored, and discharge requires collective action.
claims.task: Joint post-deployment review of subgroup performance across the four organisations.
claims.counter: S10's model was built for global structural injustice and expressly declines to isolate perpetrators; a defendant will say it therefore cannot ground concrete enforceable duties for a licensed device, and S8 will add that no gap has been shown at all.
claims.reason: E17 and E12 show the diffusion directly; the counter limits what the claim can do (it grounds a joint review, not a damages allocation), which is why the claim is stated at that level only.

sources.reference: ENGR4960J Assignment 2 brief - AI medical recommendation case (instructor-provided)
sources.note: Source of all given facts. S1-S10 are added at G2; no literature is cited at G1.

sources.reference: Elish, M. C. (2019). Moral crumple zones: Cautionary tales in human-robot interaction. Engaging Science, Technology, and Society, 5, 40-60.
sources.note: Supports the claim that responsibility migrates to the nearest human operator who had limited control, quoted from the Abstract and the Introduction; limitation: a qualitative comparative case study that diagnoses misattribution but supplies no normative rule for correct allocation, and the supplied PDF text layer carries no page numerals, so it is cited by section only.

sources.reference: Johnson, D. G. (2020). Engineering ethics: Contemporary and enduring debates. Yale University Press.
sources.note: Supports the rotten-apples-and-rotten-barrels reading of mishaps and the separation of accountability, blameworthiness and liability, quoted at p. 118 and from the section Sorting Out Responsibility; limitation: only the page numerals 118 and 119 survive in the supplied file, so the later passages are section-anchored, and the chapter is a case synthesis rather than an argument about AI.

sources.reference: Luegenbiehl, H. C., & Clancy, R. F. (2017). Global engineering ethics. Butterworth-Heinemann.
sources.note: Supports the anti-scapegoating thesis, that converging causal conditions make it unfair to place all responsibility on single actors, quoted at pp. 84, 86 and 87; limitation: the available pages concern Hurricane Katrina rather than AI or medicine, and the thesis can immunise organisations against accountability if read too strongly.

sources.reference: Matthias, A. (2004). The responsibility gap: Ascribing responsibility for the actions of learning automata. Ethics and Information Technology, 6(3), 175-183.
sources.note: Supports the founding claim that learning automata make future behaviour unpredictable and that reduced control reduces responsibility, quoted from the Abstract and the Introduction; limitation: the supplied PDF has no page numerals so it is cited by section, S6 holds that it covers only the culpability gap, and its own lung-cancer example concedes that blame is possible where limitations were known beforehand.

sources.reference: Reijers, W., Young, M. T., & Coeckelbergh, M. (2025). Introduction to the ethics of emerging technologies. Palgrave Macmillan.
sources.note: Supports the claim that responsibility presupposes capacity and institutional support and that innovation outruns regulation, quoted at pp. 85 and 86; limitation: an introductory chapter that asserts the gap at the level of innovation governance and offers no operational criterion for who must verify post-deployment performance.

sources.reference: Santoni de Sio, F., & Mecacci, G. (2021). Four responsibility gaps with artificial intelligence: Why they matter and how to address them. Philosophy & Technology, 34, 1057-1084.
sources.note: Supports the four-way taxonomy of culpability, moral accountability, public accountability and active responsibility, and the many-hands point, quoted at pp. 1059, 1065, 1066, 1073 and 1077; limitation: a conceptual framework that assumes the gap it taxonomises and presents meaningful human control as programmatic future work, which is exactly what S8 rejects.

sources.reference: Santoni de Sio, F., & van den Hoven, J. (2018). Meaningful human control over autonomous systems: A philosophical account. Frontiers in Robotics and AI, 5, Article 15.
sources.note: Supports the requirement that supervision be real rather than nominal, through the tracking and tracing conditions, quoted from the Abstract and the section Meaningful Human Control: Tracking and Tracing; limitation: the journal uses article locators and the PDF has no page numerals, the account originates in lethal autonomous weapons and is extended to civil systems only programmatically, and traceability to a human does not by itself establish that the human could act.

sources.reference: Tigard, D. W. (2021). There is no techno-responsibility gap. Philosophy & Technology, 34, 589-607.
sources.note: Supports the counter-argument that a technology-specific responsibility gap is a prevailing assumption rather than a demonstrated fact, quoted from the Abstract and section 1 Introduction; limitation: the supplied file retains only the page numeral 590 so it is cited by section, the author sets legal liability aside, and he analyses ascription to agents without offering a design or institutional criterion, so he does not reach active-responsibility or public-accountability gaps.

sources.reference: van de Poel, I., & Royakkers, L. (2011). Ethics, technology, and engineering: An introduction. Wiley-Blackwell.
sources.note: Supports the four conditions of blameworthiness, the demanding foreseeability standard and the treatment of a failure to act as causal contribution, quoted at pp. 9 and 12; limitation: the supplied PDF contains chapter 1 only, so the whitelist pages 252-267 are absent and this source is not used for the hierarchy and organization or forward-looking models, and the book is an introductory text oriented to individual agents.

sources.reference: Young, I. M. (2006). Responsibility and global justice: A social connection model. Social Philosophy and Policy, 23(1), 102-130.
sources.note: Supports the shared and forward-looking social connection model and the five features that distinguish it from the liability model, quoted at p. 103; limitation: the model was built for global labour justice, it supplements rather than replaces the liability model, and it deliberately declines to isolate perpetrators, which limits what it can ground for a licensed medical device.
